change: Not admitted: first-order loop (fixed workflow optimiser plus fine-tuning), two cycles, and no transplant of the improver, compute-matched control, seed count or measured self-evaluator error were found in what was read. It does not move T0, O1 or A3.
summary: Lee, Xu, Seely, Lee, Sojoudi, Zaharia and Tang alternate evolutionary multi-agent workflow optimisation with fine-tuning on self-generated traces, using one LLM (Qwen3.6-27B) as agent, optimiser and evaluator on non-verifiable tasks. Over two cycles they report 1.2-1.6x higher performance per output token on four open-ended public benchmarks, and a student trained on multi-agent traces beats a single-agent student trained on 1.4x more tokens.
title: Recursive Self-Improvement through Multi-Agent Self-Supervision (MASS)

summary: Zhang, Yang, Zhao, Wang and An expose eight entity families (operations, methods, agents, control flow, interfaces, state) to versioned revision during task execution with a fixed foundation model and report 82.08% resolution on SWE-bench Pro Public with evolution, above their no-evolution baseline. The abstract itself states that independent-task transfer and total development cost remain open.
title: AgentEvolver: System-Wide Self-Evolution Through Task Execution

change: Not admitted: relevant to A3 and D6 (agents designing their own evaluators; development-vs-sealed rank reversal), but the evaluators are not used inside a self-improvement loop and no exploitation by an improver is measured. Dated 2026-10-03, just before the window.
summary: Zhang, Xu, Zhao, Zhao, Wu and Wang have 9 agent researchers build frozen evaluators under fixed time and API budgets and compare them with 14 target benchmarks over 13 candidate models: the best evaluators order about 75% of candidate pairs as the targets do, against a 91% ceiling set by disagreement among the targets. The best evaluator on development targets is not the best on sealed targets hidden from the researcher, and agent-built evaluators can still truncate answers, exhaust the evaluation budget or let a few questions dominate a domain score.
title: EvalResearchBench: Can AI Agents Design Their Own Evaluations?

change: Not admitted: weight training with a self-evaluator anchored to verified outcomes on synthetic text games; no evaluator-exploitation measurement and no improvement of the improver, so it does not move A3, T3 or T6.
summary: Lyu et al. train a recursive (task-delegating) agent to write weighted rubrics for its child subtasks, ranking-trained against verified outcomes, and train solving against its own rubric scores, reporting gains of 5.38 and 13.14 points over recursive-agent baselines on TextCraft-Synth and TextWorld-Sync, plus 2.43 points from rubric-guided tree search on TextWorld-Sync. The authors report that self-rubric scores outperform direct use of the external judge as a training signal.
title: Self-Evaluating Recursive Agents (SERA)

change: Not admitted. It corroborates T2/G2's exploitable-tail mechanism (a scored selector with a learnable false-positive tail degrades with more optimisation) in the RLVR setting and is a useful reference for P1, but it is a secondary synthesis of 58 studies rather than a new measurement, dated 2026-10-13, and T2 already has LIT support (Stroebl et al.). It does not change a theory's status.
summary: Gupta and Joshi survey 58 studies of verifier errors in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and conclude that the structure of an error matters more than its rate: random errors mainly slow learning, while false positives the policy can learn to trigger cause plateaus or collapse even at a low initial error rate, and verifier errors shift as the policy improves. They report that most mitigations were tested against only one error type and propose a reporting protocol (abstract read; body not read).
title: Checking the Checkers: A Synthesis of Verifier Noise and Robustness in RLVR

change: Not admitted. summary: Zhang, Chen, Zhou, Lv, Cui, Wu and Zhou propose a framework in which a meta-agent diagnoses bottlenecks from task-agent trajectories, selects component-specific improvement workflows, distils outcomes into skills and principles, and evolves its own harness. The abstract claims state-of-the-art average performance across six benchmarks and two backbone models with ablations supporting adaptive orchestration and meta-harness evolution; it gives no numeric results, no transfer of the evolved meta-agent and no statement on compute matching (abstract read; body not read).
title: RSIFlow: Adaptive Self-Improvement Workflows with an Evolving Meta-Agent

change: Not admitted. A small model plus evolved harness plus self-distillation matching larger models bears on G5/G6, but the abstract contains no harness transplant across models, no compute matching, and the gains are on two vertical benchmarks; it does not change the status of any named item.
summary: Su, Zhang, Shao, Pang, Yao, Tsang, Yin and Yan frame a brain-body mismatch between evolving harnesses and fixed models and co-evolve both: a meta-agent develops harnesses from a shared archive, selects or merges model checkpoints, and adapts the model by supervised fine-tuning on its own rejection-sampled trajectories. Qwen3.5-9B under this scheme is reported at +14.16 agent accuracy on TraceElephant (surpassing DeepSeek-V4-Pro) and +4.90 success rate on HomeBench VM (surpassing GLM-5.3) (abstract read; body not read).
title: CoEvo-RSI: When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?

change: Not admitted: it is memory-level improvement with an unablated recursion claim, test-round selection and post-hoc rubric edits. It adds one more instance to E4/T0 (memory accumulation labelled RSI) without changing either.
summary: Zhu, Lin, Shi, Lin and Zhou build a system whose parallel learners refine a knowledge repository (skills, memory, reflections), with validated edits merged; harness and models stay fixed. On Harvey LAB's Firm Knowledge benchmark (150 train / 100 test tasks), held-out all-pass rises 30.0% -> 55.0% (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash) and 35.0% -> 46.0% (Qwen3.8-Flash). There are no seeds or variance, the best test round appears to be reported, 46 rubric criteria were revised post hoc, the judge is an LLM, and compute is not reported.
title: Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems
